newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson to take witness stand in civil trial.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson to take witness stand in civil trial.

text.p: Nearly 2-1/2 years after his ex-wife and her friend were murdered, O.J. Simpson will take the witness stand for the first time on Friday and tell a court what he was doing the night of the killings.

A bid by Simpson to put his testimony back to next week failed on Thursday in a Santa Monica court when Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki ruled that the former football star should take the witness stand on Friday.

Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, said Simpson had spent the week in a suburban court, where he is fighting for custody of his two young children, and he wanted the extra time to "allow Mr. Simpson to get his head on straight before these lawyers (for the plaintiffs) start attacking him."

Simpson was found not guilty by a criminal court jury in October last year of the June 12, 1994 murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman. He is being sued by the families of the victims in a wrongful death case in which they are seeking financial damages.

Simpson, who did not testify at his criminal trial, was expected to remain on the witness stand next Monday and Tuesday. His testimony will be the first time he has publicly related under oath his movements on the night of the murders.
"This will be the defining moment of the trial," said Peter Arenella, a law professor at the University of California at Los Angeles.

Despite his acquittal on the double-murder charges at his criminal trial, Simpson has been battling since to clear his name in the court of public opinion, where a majority of white Americans disagreed with the jury's not-guilty verdict.
The verdict split Americans along racial lines, with most blacks believing Simpson's defence team theory that the black athlete was framed by police.

When he takes the stand in the Santa Monica courtroom where the civil trial has been under way for just over two months, Simpson will have to tell jurors his alibi for the night of June 12, 1994. He has already given a sworn deposition saying he flew to Chicago that night and was notified there by Los Angeles police that his ex-wife had been slashed to death outside her home. Goldman was killed as well.

Simpson is being called to the stand by the families' attorneys, who hope to catch him in inconsistencies about his movements the night of the murders. Simpson's lawyers will have a chance to ask questions and attempt to undo any damage.

"This is pivotal in the case. Everyone wants to hear from O.J.," Laurie Levenson, a professor at Loyola University Law School, said. But she said putting a defendant on the stand was always a risk for either side.
"He is a dangerous witness. He has a natural charm that he has used effectively. The plaintiffs need to show he was capable of such rage that he could kill two people," she said.
Levenson said Simpson's attorneys will have coached him on how to act on the stand. He had plenty of practice this summer when he was grilled by lawyers during a 10-day deposition.

"It is not likely he will snap," she said, adding that the plaintiffs will try to point out differences between Simpson's statements to police, his deposition and accounts he has given in a book and on a video.

"They will try and catch him in little inconsistencies, like how he got the cuts on his hand, statements that he had never hit Nicole, the Bronco flight," Levenson said, referring to the slow-speed chase on which Simpson led police along southern California freeways before he was arrested.

Simpson's former house guest Brian "Kato" Kaelin testified on Tuesday he and Simpson had watched a video containing a scene about oral sex, which Simpson compared to an act he witnessed his ex-wife performing on another man. Levenson said this could be used to portray him as a man with an obsession.

The defence tactic, she predicted, would be to paint him as so upset at the loss of his ex-wife that he could not remember the exact details of his movements that night. "They will try and point the finger back at Nicole with O.J. saying: 'I was a caring and loving husband. I loved her so much.'"
